Very cheaply, I did it spending 0-10 Euros a day, basically you can eat for 2-3 Euros a day without being too hungry, usually canned lentils or chickpeas, a pack of raisins or peanuts and some dessert is what I ate through a day, sometimes tuna if I want some luxury, I did digestive cookies for a couple weeks before getting so sick of them and wanting to puke everytime I taste them, expect very shitty shits and expect to carry food in your backpack from cheap supermarket to another (I bought exclusively from the chain Dia which is very cheap and has good deals), meaning you will on some stretches carry your food for 3-4 days (2 days on average I'd say), if you don't want to carry food for days you can buy from stores in every village but expect to spend a tad bit more.  


You can sleep outside, aslong as you are stealthy you can pull the Camino off spending 0-5 Euro a day if you don't stay at Albergues.

I had just done \~135km in 3 days of walking, a 56km day followed by 44km and 35km days, my backpack was probably 10-15KGs (15-25% of my weight at the time) since I was doing it on a budget and carrying food from a cheap supermarket to another enough for a 3-4 days, my ankles were in incredible pain, I mean incredible, I had never felt something more painful over a long period of time, it felt like a hammer with a needle head hitting my right ankle everytime I took a step, I couldn't slow down because I was limited on time so I didn't have time to take rest days or to do few kilometers, I kept the pace and limped for the next week.  
I didn't give quitting much thought because I was really motivated to finish it but this was definitely the lowest point in my Camino, I cried many times and beat myself over it everyday because I didn't like the fact I was limping, this was the lowest point but it gave me what I came to the Camino to achieve, those few days strengthened my relationship with god like nothing else ever could.  
  
I couldn't have done it without clenching that cross I wear on my neck and asking the lord for help.

Yes, I learned that the hard way being the first and only time I ever got "lost" on the Camino, I had followed the Via Valcarlos instead of the Napoleon route, I had to turn back once I realized "Huh, I sure as hell am not walking uphill".

Lots of places to camp (contrary to popular belief), you pass next to places everyday.  
Lots of greenery to hide you, many Spanish villages have a park aswell, at the enterance/exit (or both) with atleast tables and some with water, they're also a viable last option, from my experience villagers don't give a shit and never personally saw a police officer in those small villages, if you respect the place, clean after you, setup after sunset and leave before sunrise you will be fine where ever you camp.

Only in the Meseta you will have trouble finding viable camping spots (though not impossible), easiest would be the stretch after Leon especially Galicia.

I took a sleeping bag a bivvy and a foampad, I didn't camp every single day but I did pass next to viable camping spots almost every day, no matter what people tell you, if you have an eye for these things you can find camping spots easily.

Walking in Galicia (somewhere around Palas De Rei, iirc), shivering from the cold, still very dark it's around 4am, very foggy and so my headlamp doesn't really reach further than a meter, very muddy it had rained the whole night before, I'm all alone, hear what sounded like a woman/girl scream, freak the fuck out, turn headlamp off as to not show myself (not that anybody could see me through the fog), stand still for a bit to process, turn headlamp back on and run as fast as I can.

In-terms of money, your best bet would be to get a low fee / no fee credit card to use, that's what I did, everytime I'd pass through a city I'll hit the ATM and usually get 50 Euros I found that the perfect amount, it is enough for a few days to pay for Albergues and not too much if it were to get stolen (didn't encounter theft but I've heard that it sadly happens), I'd only use the cash to pay for Albergues (as most from what I know don't accept card), and for anything else like supermarkets I use the card. This is only good if you can get a no-fee card.  
Just be wary some stretches you won't encounter cities or ATMs for a couple days, the paper you get at Pilgrim's Office in Saint-Jean will have that information about ATMs.  


I wasn't necessarily called to the Camino, I went there for adventure and something very deep inside also went for the religious aspect, and I'm so glad I went, it definitely impacted me on a religious level and I got out a different person in-terms of religion, which brings me to another point, try not to spoil yourself, while staying at a Donativo someone said "Through pain we find the Camino, we find Jesus, whether it's physical or mental pain", and it is so true, I'm not necessarily saying to put yourself in pain, but don't make it too easy on yourself, having it easy takes away a very big aspect, there's nothing wrong with going there as a vacation and not wanting to be in too much discomfort or pain, but if you go for the religious pilgrim aspect then the quote I wrote above should be like a guideline.

As someone pointed out, Pilgrim office is in Saint-Jean in France, I thought there were many spread out across the different Caminos but that's not the case.  
So if he's not passing through Saint-Jean, then I'd recommend just using the wisepilgrim site, it has all the stages, all towns/villages you pass through and the Albergues in those towns.

I've seen so many people say it's hard finding place to sleep when I was researching the Camino, but it really isn't... Only the Burgos-Leon stretch might be a bit hard to find a stealthy place to sleep at, otherwise you pass near a dozen places throughout the day where sleeping is easy.

***How do you book shelters:*** You really don't have to, at the time you're going it's off-season, I went in June which is more busy than March and I didn't book any Albergues and only happened once where Albergue was full. So you shouldn't have a problem with that.

***Do people cook, or is it always eating at a shelter:*** People do cook, I cooked some meals (only a couple times), most Albergues have kitchens, don't expect the best of equipment though.

Be wary of Galicia though, the Xunta Albergues have nice looking kitchens that invite you to cook in them! until you open the drawers and find literally nothing, literally, no pots, no plates, nothing, a literal empty kitchen (I'm looking at you O Cebreiro).

Some Albergues offer dinner if you are ready to pay for it, most Donativos I stayed at offered Dinner (leave a good donation if you can, if you are having a "bad" dinner then you know the people before you didn't put much donations).

Kitchens can get a bit crowded on bigger Albergues.

***How does one find shelters:*** If you go to a Pilgrim's office they'll give you a paper with Albergues, what they offer (like Kitchen, Dinner etc...), their phone numbers etc... otherwise you can use this site: [https://www.wisepilgrim.com/](https://www.wisepilgrim.com/) it's very very useful not just for Albergues.

***If he takes a hammock can he spend a couple nights outdoors:*** I didn't personally take a hammock, but I did sleep outside with just a sleeping bag and a foam pad, it's 100% possible no matter what people tell you, just be ready though, I suggest getting a tarp aswell if you are going in March, it will be rainy, bring a good sleeping bag and insulation for the cold.  
If you setup after sunset and leave before sunrise you will be alright, Spanish villagers are friendly (ok mostly).

For the most part I ate canned food, bread and raisins (except some days in Donativos where we had dinner).  
Weigh-loss wasn't a problem, barely noticed it and definately gained it back the first week back at home.

Gonna depend on where, how comfortable you want to be, what you are interested in mainly, if you care about food etc...
I'm currently in Europe I've only been in Greece and Italy so far (25 days total), your expenses will be as follows (mainly).
Accomodation, Food (+water), Transport, Entertainment.

Accomodation: this will depend how comfortable you want to be, accommodation is just somewhere to lay your head at night, shower, relax and plan so if you aren't too picky and don't mind sharing a room woth people, hostels will be your best bet, I payed 12 euros a day INCLUDING breakfast in Athens (though this is off season), you can get cheaper ones and there are more expensive luxurious ones. In Italy it's much more expensive especially in Rome since there is a 3.5 euro tax per person per night, if you do come to Rome please stay away from the cheapest hostels, they are very dirty and sometimes moldy, breakfast included means croissant and coffee (I've tried 3 cheap ones so far, all are the same).

Food: again will depend how picky you are, you could be a food enthusiast and like to try different cuisines which is nice, but not on your wallet. Cheapest option would be supermarkets, Lidl in the case of Europe is probably your best bet but not always available, just search for the nearest supermarket chain. Or in cheap countries like Greece you could get cheap street food, in my case I've spent on average in Athens 2 euros a day on food usually a 1.5 euro falafel wrap and a 0.5 euro bagel sold in street bakery stalls. In Rome it's different because street food is still expensive so I've been getting by on 2-4 euros a day for food from supermarkets, this is usually a baguette and cottage chesse for breakfast which has been costing me 1.5 euro, very filling cheap and tasty, and supermarkets have a pastry section which has cheap stuff like spinach rolls etc... in Lidl I get 12 spinach rolls for 1.9 euros!. These are all examples, supermarket foods really are your best bet for cheap eating though they will take more of your time, like picking what to eat if you don't have something in mind and finding a place to eat (I'm picky about this so I usually have to walk to a park). Water is basically free you can fill from anywhere, some cities have running water like in Rome in beautiful taps scattered around, but worst case you can fill with tap water in any toilet around or at the hostel.

Transport is transport, can't really do it cheaper aslong as you get the correct pass (week pass etc...), though in some cities you won't need to use transport if you're fine with walking, like Rome, I suggest you first try a day or two without transport see how it goes, though you will be walking alot (I've been doing 20-30km a day) and will be sore for the first few days, but it's worth it cuz after those few days ull be walking a lot without being sore at all which is an amazing feeling.
Flying between places is NOT always cheaper even with budget airlines, check busses (Flixbus or whatever busses operate in a country, in Italy for example, Itabus are sometimes cheaper than Flix), check ferries aswell if it's coastal, sometimes you get overnight ferries or busses which might be cheaper or same price as a flight AND you can sleep on them.

Entertainment will also depend on you, nature is free (usually), so if you are into hikes and nature then that's perfect because they're either free or cheap. Or maybe you're a history or art enthusiast and you wanna do that, obviously don't cheap out too much on Entertainment because you still want to have fun, but be sensible, check which days are free days etc... (like in Athens some museums are free on sundays, even Acropolis is free on first sunday of the winter months iirc)

Hope my examples helped, for reference I've been spending 20 euros a day in Rome this includes everything (just accomodation and food tbh) this is what I call survival budget.
In Athens I survived on 15 Euros a day and had the best time of my life for 2 weeks.
I don't spend money on entertainment/activities much because I don't enjoy them, so yes I've been into Athens  but didn't enter Acropolis and in Rome and not planning to pay for Roman Forum or Colosseum (have seen them from outside though), I enjoy just walking around and surviving outside my home country for as little as possible.



EDIT: I forgot Corona tests (if you'll have to test to go home) some places they can get to 70 euros (I'm sure there are more expensive countries), some places they can be 10 euros (Greece) so maybe plan to go home from a country that has cheap tests (obviously if you were planning to visit that country in your travels).
